opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a lot of what makes Operator useful in practice is that the web is really heterogeneous. Every site has its own little quirks — where the search bar lives, how the checkout flow works, whether there's a pop-up you need to dismiss, which filters actually do what you'd expect. The underlying model is pretty good at figuring that stuff out on the fly, but "pretty good at figuring it out" means it's spending steps exploring, and sometimes it takes a wrong turn.

Site-specific instructions let you front-load that knowledge. If you use a particular site all the time — say you always order groceries from the same place, or you book travel through a specific airline — you can just tell Operator, "When you're on this site, here's how I like things done," or "Always check this box," or "My preferred seat is an aisle." It's a lot like onboarding a new assistant. The first week, they're asking you a bunch of questions. Once you've told them how you like things, they just get it right.

So from a user's perspective, it does two things. One, it makes the agent more reliable on the tasks you actually repeat, which is where most of the value is. And two, it makes it more personalized — it's not just completing the task generically, it's completing it the way *you* would. And honestly, I think that's a pattern we'll see more of with agents generally: the raw capability matters, but a lot of the practical value comes from giving the agent the right context about you and the environment it's operating in.

r001.rationale: It says instructions let users front-load knowledge about a site’s quirks and preferences, guiding Operator through website tasks.

r002.rationale: It says the instructions make Operator more reliable on tasks users repeat, communicating more consistent performance across those tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that a general-purpose agent like Operator is kind of in a weird spot when it lands on a website. It knows how to use a browser, it knows roughly what a shopping cart is or what a form looks like, but it doesn't know the quirks of your particular site. And every site has quirks, right? Where the real "add to cart" button is versus the one that opens a modal, how your checkout flow handles promo codes, what the agent should never do, like resubmitting an order if the page hangs.

So when we started playing with site-specific instructions, the thing that jumped out at me was that the agent's baseline capability was actually fine. Most of the failures weren't "the model can't reason about this." They were "the model doesn't know this one thing about this one site," and it would either guess wrong or stop and ask a clarifying question that a human who'd used the site twice would never need to ask.

Instructions let you close that gap really cheaply. You can say, "On this site, always use the search bar instead of navigating the category menus, because the menus are flaky." Or, "Don't proceed past the payment page without confirming with the user." That's a couple of sentences, and it turns a task that succeeded sixty percent of the time into one that succeeds basically every time.

The other piece, which I think people underrate, is that it shifts where the knowledge lives. Instead of trying to bake every site's idiosyncrasies into the model's weights, which is never going to keep up with how fast websites change, you let the people who actually know the site, whether that's the site owner or a power user, write it down. It's a bit like the difference between hiring a smart new employee and hiring a smart new employee and also handing them the onboarding doc. Same person, wildly different first week.

And from a reliability standpoint, I like it because it's inspectable. If the agent does something dumb, you can look at the instructions and ask, did we tell it the wrong thing, or did we just not tell it? That's a much easier debugging loop than staring at a trajectory and trying to infer what the model was thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator lacks knowledge of a particular site’s quirks and that site-specific instructions fill that gap with guidance for completing tasks.

r002.rationale: It says instructions can turn a task’s success rate from 60% to basically every time, directly describing more repeatable performance.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is that a lot of what you need to know to use a website effectively isn’t obvious from looking at the page. You might know where a particular setting lives, or that you have to go through a certain sequence of steps to get something done. Without that context, Operator has to figure it out as it goes.

Site-specific instructions let you give it that knowledge up front. You can say, “On this site, here’s the workflow I use, and here’s what a successful result looks like.” That takes some of the guesswork out of the task and helps it get to the result you actually want more consistently.

r001.rationale: It says site-specific instructions give Operator up-front knowledge of a site’s workflow and successful result, including guidance that is not obvious from the page.

r002.rationale: It says the instructions reduce guesswork and help Operator reach the desired result more consistently, communicating more repeatable performance.

sol-6.1.text: I think site-specific instructions are helpful because there’s often a gap between what you want to accomplish and how a particular website expects you to do it. You might know that there’s a certain filter you need to set, or that the information you want is tucked away in a particular tab. Giving Operator that context means it doesn’t have to rediscover those details every time. And if you have preferences for how it should use that site, you can make those explicit, so you get more consistent results with less back-and-forth.

r001.rationale: It explains that site-specific context fills the gap between the user's goal and a website's expected workflow, including filters or tabs Operator might otherwise need to rediscover.

r002.rationale: It says explicit site preferences lead to more consistent results, communicating more repeatable performance.
